questions.question: A student says the function of a capacitor in the circuit is to store electric charge. Explain why this is not a complete description of its function.
questions.answer: A capacitor also stores energy and releases it over time; with the resistor it controls the rate at which the p.d. and current decay, through the time constant RC.
steps: A charged capacitor stores energy, E = 0.5 Q V = 0.5 C V^2, not just charge.
When the supply is removed, the stored energy is released as a current through the resistor.
The rate of release is set by the time constant RC, so the p.d. decays gradually rather than instantly.
This controlled release is what gives the night light its slow fade, so the complete function is to store and release energy at a controlled rate.

questions.question: Show that the p.d. V across the capacitor during charging is V = V0 - V0 e^(-t/RC), where V0 is the e.m.f., R the resistance and C the capacitance.
steps: Kirchhoff's voltage law: V0 = I R + q / C, where q / C is the p.d. across the capacitor.
The current is I = dq / dt, so V0 = R dq/dt + q / C.
Rearranging: dq/dt = (C V0 - q) / (RC), which has solution q = C V0 (1 - e^(-t/RC)).
The capacitor p.d. is V = q / C = V0 (1 - e^(-t/RC)) = V0 - V0 e^(-t/RC).

As the capacitor charges, VC rises, so VR = V0 - VC falls.

questions.question: Show that the p.d. VC across the capacitor is given by VC = V0 (1 - e^(-t/RC)), where R is the resistance and C the capacitance. The integrated circuit has infinite resistance.
steps: Infinite resistance of the integrated circuit means no current flows through it, so the same current flows through R and C.
Kirchhoff: V0 = I R + q / C with I = dq / dt, giving dq/dt = (C V0 - q) / (RC).
Solving with q = 0 at t = 0 gives q = C V0 (1 - e^(-t/RC)).
So VC = q / C = V0 (1 - e^(-t/RC)).

questions.question: Which of the following units is equivalent to the farad? A: C V^-1; B: J V^-1; C: s^-1; D: s J^-1.

steps: Capacitance is defined as C = Q / V.

questions.question: When the p.d. across a capacitor is V, the energy stored is W. Select the energy stored when the p.d. is 2V.
questions.answer: D: 4W.
steps: Energy stored by a capacitor is W = 0.5 C V^2, which depends on V squared.
With the p.d. doubled, the energy becomes 0.5 C (2V)^2 = 4 x (0.5 C V^2) = 4W.
So the answer is option D, 4W.

questions.question: A capacitor discharges through a resistor with time constant 5 s. Select the time for the charge on the plates to halve.
questions.answer: D: 5 ln2 s (about 3.5 s).
steps: Charge decays as Q = Q0 e^(-t/RC) = Q0 e^(-t/5).
Halving the charge requires e^(-t/5) = 0.5.
Taking logarithms gives t / 5 = ln 2, so t = 5 ln2 s, which is option D.

questions.question: A light conducting sphere of radius r = 3.5 cm is charged by touching one of two plates separated by d = 5.0 cm with a potential difference of 4500 V. The sphere has capacitance C = 4 pi epsilon0 r. Calculate the electrostatic force on the sphere.
questions.answer: Electrostatic force = 1.6 x 10^-3 N.
steps: Capacitance of the sphere C = 4 pi epsilon0 r = 1.11 x 10^-10 x 0.035 = 3.89 x 10^-12 F.
On touching the 4500 V plate the sphere takes the plate potential, so Q = C V = 3.89 x 10^-12 x 4500 = 1.75 x 10^-8 C.
The field between the plates is E = V / d = 4500 / 0.050 = 9.0 x 10^4 V m^-1.
The electrostatic force on the sphere is F = Q E = 1.75 x 10^-8 x 9.0 x 10^4 = 1.6 x 10^-3 N.

questions.question: After charging, the conducting sphere oscillates between the two plates, touching each alternately. Explain why it oscillates.
questions.answer: On touching a plate the sphere takes that plate's charge, is then repelled by it and attracted to the opposite plate, where it loses charge and repeats the cycle.
steps: The sphere touches the positive plate, gains positive charge, and is repelled from that plate.
The sphere is then attracted to the negative plate across the gap.
On contact with the negative plate, it gains negative charge (neutralising its positive charge), so it is repelled back.
The sequence of attraction, contact and repulsion repeats, so the sphere oscillates between the plates.

questions.question: In Franklin's version, one bell is earthed and the other is connected to a positively charged lightning conductor. The sphere is initially uncharged. Explain why the sphere starts to move between the bells.
questions.answer: The positive bell induces a negative charge on the near side of the uncharged sphere, so it is attracted; on contact it becomes positive and is then repelled to the earthed bell, and the cycle repeats.
steps: The positively charged bell polarises the uncharged sphere, inducing negative charge on its near side.
The sphere is attracted towards the positive bell and touches it.
Charge is transferred, the sphere becomes positive, and it is repelled towards the earthed bell.
On reaching the earthed bell it discharges and the cycle repeats, so the sphere moves between the bells.

questions.question: An ultracapacitor of capacitance 47 F can store a maximum charge of 56 C. It is suggested it can store 1000 times the energy of a 470 uF capacitor at 12 V. Assess the validity of this suggestion.
questions.answer: Approximately valid: the maximum energy is about 33 J against about 0.034 J, a ratio of about 990, close to 1000 (but the ultracapacitor cannot be charged to 12 V, as its maximum p.d. is only 1.2 V).
steps: Energy of the 470 uF capacitor at 12 V: E = 0.5 C V^2 = 0.5 x 470 x 10^-6 x 12^2 = 0.0338 J.
Maximum energy of the ultracapacitor: E = Q^2 / (2C) = 56^2 / (2 x 47) = 33.4 J.
Ratio = 33.4 / 0.0338 = 990, which is close to 1000, so the suggestion is approximately valid.
However the ultracapacitor's maximum p.d. is V = Q / C = 56 / 47 = 1.2 V, so it cannot store energy at 12 V; the comparison is of maximum energies only.

questions.question: A cell of p.d. V0, a capacitor, a resistor and a switch are connected, with the capacitor initially uncharged. Explain the variation of the capacitor p.d. V with time shown in the graph, referring to the charge on the capacitor and the current in the circuit.
questions.answer: The capacitor p.d. rises from zero and approaches V0 asymptotically: as charge builds up the current falls, so the rate of charging falls and the gradient decreases to zero.
steps: Initially the capacitor is uncharged, so V = 0 and the whole p.d. V0 appears across the resistor; the current is at its maximum, V0 / R.
Current flows onto the capacitor plates, so the charge Q on the capacitor increases with time.
V = Q / C increases as the charge increases.
As V rises, the p.d. across the resistor (V0 - V) falls, so the current falls.
A smaller current means charge arrives more slowly, so the gradient of the V-t graph decreases from its maximum at t = 0 towards zero.
The capacitor p.d. therefore approaches the cell e.m.f. V0 exponentially, with the time constant RC controlling how fast.

steps: Capacitance is C = Q / V, so V = Q / C.
